# M05 — Regime-aware models (Phase 5)

*Generated by `python -m src.experiments.run_regime_lstm` on 2026-07-21 17:04 UTC. Numbers trace to `results/tables/m05_regime_dl_*` and `results/predictions/m05_regime_dl_*.parquet`.*

## Scope

Roadmap Phase 5 (Ch2 §2.5): condition the Phase-3 **LSTM** on the Phase-4 **HMM regime** signal and test whether it improves daily realized-variance forecasts on the same leakage-free anchored walk-forward as Phases 2–3 (**RQ2**). The regime signal is the **causal filtered** posterior P(sₜ|x₁..xₜ) from Phase 4 (`hmm_filt_p*`); it is lagged one day so a forecast for RVₜ only ever conditions on the regime known at t−1. Hyperparameters are fixed at the Phase-3 selection (hidden 128, lookback 10, lr 1e-3), so 'LSTM → Regime-LSTM' isolates regime-conditioning rather than a new sweep.

Two architectures (roadmap Phase 5):
- **Regime-LSTM-A** — regime as feature: filtered posteriors appended to the LSTM input (Ch2 §2.5). `Regime-LSTM-A-RVonly` is the same on HAR-RV's exact input set (RV history only), matched to the Phase-3 winner.
- **Regime-LSTM-B** — regime-specific experts: one LSTM per regime, soft-gated by the posterior at t−1 (mixture-of-experts).

## Significance — formal DM + Model Confidence Set

Pairwise **Diebold–Mariano** (1995) on the QLIKE differential, with the Harvey–Leybourne–Newbold (1997) small-sample correction and a Student-t reference (a negative statistic means the first model has the lower loss). The **Model Confidence Set** (Hansen, Lunde & Nason 2011) then controls for multiple comparison across *all* models jointly (Ch2 §2.7).

| comparison (a vs b) | DM stat | p | better | n |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Regime-LSTM-A vs LSTM | -0.56 | 0.575 | Regime-LSTM-A | 784 |
| Regime-LSTM-A vs HAR-RV | -0.77 | 0.440 | Regime-LSTM-A | 784 |
| Regime-LSTM-B vs LSTM | -2.13 | 0.034 | Regime-LSTM-B | 784 |
| Regime-LSTM-B vs HAR-RV | -1.04 | 0.298 | Regime-LSTM-B | 784 |
| Regime-LSTM-A-RVonly vs LSTM-RVonly | 0.50 | 0.616 | LSTM-RVonly | 784 |

**Model Confidence Set — 90% confidence.** QLIKE loss; stationary bootstrap (2000 reps, block 10, 'R' statistic, seed 17). Surviving set = {HAR-RV, LSTM, LSTM-RVonly, Regime-LSTM-A, Regime-LSTM-A-RVonly, Regime-LSTM-B}; eliminated = {EGARCH, GARCH, RW-RV}.

## Findings (RQ2)

The overall best model on the board is **Regime-LSTM-B** (QLIKE **0.2583**), ahead of the regime-agnostic LSTM 0.2650 and HAR-RV 0.2745. Adding the regime signal **lowers** pooled QLIKE relative to the regime-agnostic LSTM (0.2583 vs 0.2650).

This is statistically supported where it matters most: **Regime-LSTM-B** beats LSTM (DM -2.13, **p=0.034**). Against the tougher, lower-parameter HAR-RV benchmark the gap is not significant (DM -1.04, p=0.298) — consistent with the Phase-3 result and the literature that HAR-RV is hard to beat on its native target. The 90% **Model Confidence Set** retains {HAR-RV, LSTM, LSTM-RVonly, Regime-LSTM-A, Regime-LSTM-A-RVonly, Regime-LSTM-B} and rejects {EGARCH, GARCH, RW-RV}: the deep-learning/HAR cluster is statistically inseparable on 784 days, while the GARCH family and the random-walk floor are excluded outright.

**The regime signal's value is concentrated in the hard regimes — exactly the RQ2 hypothesis.** In the **crisis** state (n=70, COVID-19-dominated) every regime-aware model beats every baseline, led by **Regime-LSTM-A** (QLIKE 0.2976) vs the best baseline LSTM-RVonly (0.3193) — a **7% lower** crisis QLIKE. In the **calm** state (n=381), which dominates the pooled mean, the regime signal adds little (best regime 0.2462 vs best baseline 0.2465). The pooled average therefore *understates* the regime contribution; the per-regime table is where RQ2 is properly adjudicated.

The two architectures capture the signal differently: **Regime-LSTM-B** (mixture-of-experts) wins overall and in the transitional state, while **Regime-LSTM-A** (regime as feature) is strongest in the crisis state. The MoE trains one LSTM per regime, so the crisis expert's *effective* sample is small (crisis ≈ 8% of days), which caps its specialisation — a limitation worth stating rather than hiding, and a reason the feature approach can lead precisely in the crisis rows.

## Gate criteria

- [x] Approach A (regime-as-feature) and Approach B (regime-expert MoE) built, both on the causal filtered posterior; leakage discipline reused from Phase 3 (train-only scaling, windows end before target, gate lagged to t−1).

- [x] Four-way+ comparison vs GARCH/EGARCH/HAR-RV/RW-RV/LSTM/LSTM-RVonly on identical splits; predictions persisted.

- [x] Per-regime (calm/transitional/crisis) error breakdown — core for RQ2.

- [x] Formal Diebold–Mariano (HLN-corrected, Student-t) on the head-to-head pairs, plus a Model Confidence Set (Hansen–Lunde–Nason 2011) over all models for multiple-comparison control (Ch2 §2.7).

- [x] Milestone + figures + reproducible config snapshot.
